The war with Midian (verses 1–6)

People who carry out private revenge without a commission from God must one day answer to him.

The same is true of those who make war and devastate kingdoms because of ambition, greed or personal resentment.

But Henry distinguishes such unjust violence from an extraordinary judgment expressly authorized by God.

Instead of an earthquake, epidemic or famine, God may appoint people to carry out a sentence against a nation.

Henry maintains that ancient Israel could demonstrate such a divine commission in this case, whereas no one today can claim one like it.

Israel's wars of judgment were commanded directly by God and were accompanied by miraculous victories.

Henry understands these judgments as punishment of nations whose sin had reached its full measure. He argues that objections arise from underestimating the evil of sin, which God hates.

This is his explanation of the historical account—not permission for private vengeance or contemporary religious warfare.

Balaam dies with Midian (verses 7–12)

Israel killed Midian's kings and Balaam.

God's providence had brought Balaam to the place where the judgment fell upon him.

If he had sincerely believed the words he had spoken about Israel's happiness, he would not have continued to associate with its enemies.

The wicked schemes by which Midian tempted Israel were Balaam's own projects.

It was just, Henry says, that he perish with those who had carried them out (Hosea 4:5).

The Israelites took women and children captive, burned the towns and strongholds, and returned to camp.

Those held responsible for leading Israel into sin (verses 13–18)

The ordinary sword of war should spare women and children.

But Henry distinguishes this from what he considers the execution of a divine judicial sentence, which must distinguish between the guilty and the innocent rather than merely between adults and children.

He says that in this particular judgment the Midianite women who had led Israel into sin bore the greatest guilt.

The female children were spared and would be raised among the Israelites, where they would not lead them into idolatry.

The account illustrates the hateful nature of sin and the grave responsibility involved in drawing others into it.

Henry applies it to the Christian's struggle: we should avoid opportunities for evil and refuse to spare our own sinful desires.

He also distinguishes the ancient custom of keeping war captives as slaves from the intention to use them for sexual immorality. This reflects his description of a historical practice, not a new endorsement of slavery.

He observes that in national disasters brought by war, disease or famine, children can suffer as a result of their parents' wrongdoing.

Yet he adds that children who die before committing actual sin are provided for by God's mercy in Christ with respect to their eternal happiness.

Purification after battle (verses 19–24)

Even though the war had been commanded by God and the fighters had committed no moral fault in obeying that command, they were required to undergo ceremonial purification.

They remained outside the camp for seven days.

This kept a strong sense of revulsion toward bloodshed alive in their minds.

The captured goods were also purified because they had previously been used by the Midianites.

The distribution of the spoils (verses 25–47)

Whatever we possess, the Lord has a rightful claim upon a portion of it.

The people's share was assessed at one part in fifty, while the soldiers' share was assessed at one part in five hundred.

Henry draws a practical lesson from that difference.

People with fewer opportunities to honor God through direct personal service should be especially ready to give from their possessions.

The officers' thanksgiving offerings (verses 48–54)

Israel's victory was remarkable: a small force overcame a much larger people.

Still more remarkable, no Israelite soldier was killed or missing.

The officers brought the gold captured in battle as an offering to the Lord.

In doing so, they acknowledged that even while serving God, they had no claim to a reward based on personal merit.

They needed forgiveness for anything sinful that had occurred.

They also wanted to express gratitude that their lives had been preserved, although they might justly have been taken away.

Verses 1-6
All who, without commission from God, dare to execute private revenge, and who, from ambition, covetousness, or resentment, wage war and desolate kingdoms, must one day answer for it. But if God, instead of sending an earthquake, a pestilence, or a famine, be pleased to authorize and command any people to avenge his cause, such a commission surely is just and right. The Israelites could show such a commission, though no persons now can do so. Their wars were begun and carried on expressly by Divine direction, and they were enabled to conquer by miracles. Unless it can be proved that the wicked Canaanites did not deserve their doom, objectors only prove their dislike to God, and their love to his enemies. Man makes light of the evil of sin, but God abhors it. This explains the terrible executions of the nations which had filled the measure of their sins.
[Num.31.7-Num.31.12]
Verses 7-12
The Israelites slew the Kings of Midian. They slew Balaam. God's overruling providence brought him thither, and their just vengeance found him. Had he himself rightly believed what he had said of the happy state of Israel, he would not have thus herded with the enemies of Israel. The Midianites' wicked wiles were Balaam's projects: it was just that he should perish with them, [Hos.4.5] Ho 4:5. They took the women and children captives. They burnt their cities and castles, and returned to the camp.
[Num.31.13-Num.31.18]
Verses 13-18
The sword of war should spare women and children; but the sword of justice should know no distinction, but that of guilty or not guilty. This war was the execution of a righteous sentence upon a guilty nation, in which the women were the worst criminals. The female children were spared, who, being brought up among the Israelites, would not tempt them to idolatry. The whole history shows the hatefulness of sin, and the guilt of tempting others; it teaches us to avoid all occasions of evil, and to give no quarter to inward lusts. The women and children were not kept for sinful purposes, but for slaves, a custom every where practised in former times, as to captives. In the course of providence, when famine and plagues visit a nation for sin, children suffer in the common calamity. In this case parents are punished in their children; and for children dying before actual sin, full provision is made as to their eternal happiness, by the mercy of God in Christ.
[Num.31.19-Num.31.24]
Verses 19-24
The Israelites had to purify themselves according to the law, and to abide without the camp seven days, though they had not contracted any moral guilt, the war being just and lawful, and commanded by God. Thus God would preserve in their minds a dread and detestation of shedding blood. The spoil had been used by Midianites, and being now come into the possession of Israelites, it was fit that it should be purified.
[Num.31.25-Num.31.47]
Verses 25-47
Whatever we have, God justly claims a part. Out of the people's share God required one in fifty, but out of the soldiers' share only one in five hundred. The less opportunity we have of honouring God with personal services, the more should we give in money or value.
[Num.31.48-Num.31.54]
Verses 48-54
The success of the Israelites had been very remarkable, so small a company overcoming such multitudes, but it was still more wonderful that not one was slain or missing. They presented the gold they found among the spoils, as an offering to the Lord. Thus they confessed, that instead of claiming a reward for their service, they needed forgiveness of much that had been amiss, and desired to be thankful for the preservation of their lives, which might justly have been taken away.

Reuben and Gad ask for land east of the Jordan (verses 1–5)

The tribes of Reuben and Gad wanted the land Israel had recently conquered to become their own inheritance.

Two ordinary human temptations may have influenced them: the lust of the eyes and the pride of life.

They valued their own convenience more highly than the good of the whole community.

Many people still do something similar.

They pursue what benefits them personally rather than what advances the cause of Jesus Christ.

They allow worldly advantage to satisfy them, instead of seeking the heavenly Canaan toward which God's people are traveling.

Moses rebukes their request (verses 6–15)

The proposal suggested that they had little regard for Canaan, distrusted God's promise and wished to avoid the dangers of conquering the land.

Moses was rightly angry.

God's people should never remain comfortable and unconcerned while their brothers and sisters face difficult or dangerous work.

That duty applies both to the needs of the whole community and to those of individuals.

Moses reminded Reuben and Gad of the fatal consequences of Israel's earlier unbelief, when their fathers had also been close to entering Canaan.

If people seriously considered how sin ends, they would be far more afraid to begin it.

The tribes promise to assist their brothers (verses 16–27)

Moses' plain rebuke achieved a good result.

When their sin and its danger were shown to them, the tribes responded to their duty without resentment or pointless argument.

Everyone should care about the well-being of others as well as personal interests.

The law of love requires us, when needed, to work, take risks and suffer for one another.

The men of war promised to go fully armed before Israel into Canaan and not return until the conquest was finished.

Moses accepted their proposal.

But he warned them that breaking their promise would be a sin against the Lord, not merely a wrong against the other tribes.

God would call them to account.

“Be sure your sin will find you out.”

Sooner or later wrongdoing catches up with the person who committed it.

Our concern should be to find out our sins now—to recognize, repent of and abandon them—before they come to find us in judgment.

The tribes settle east of the river (verses 28–42)

The tribes built up their cities—that is, they repaired what was already there.

They also changed their names.

Henry thinks the old names may have been connected with idolatry and therefore deserved to be forgotten.

Selfishness, the desire to seek our own interests instead of those of Christ, is a common and dangerous attitude.

Someone who truly believes the gospel, recognizes God's goodness, is constrained by Christ's love and is made holy through the Holy Spirit cannot remain indifferent to the spread of faith or the spiritual welfare of others merely from love of comfort or fear of hardship.

Let your light shine before other people, so that they see your good works and give glory to your Father in heaven.

Here is a proposal made by the Reubenites and Gadites, that the land lately conquered might be allotted to them. Two things common in the world might lead these tribes to make this choice; the lust of the eye, and the pride of life. There was much amiss in the principle they went upon; they consulted their own private convenience more than the public good. Thus to the present time, many seek their own things more than the things of Jesus Christ; and are led by worldly interests and advantages to take up short of the heavenly Canaan.
[Num.32.6-Num.32.15]
Verses 6-15
The proposal showed disregard to the land of Canaan, distrust of the Lord's promise, and unwillingness to encounter the difficulties and dangers of conquering and driving out the inhabitants of that land. Moses is wroth with them. It will becomes any of God's Israel to sit down unconcerned about the difficult and perilous concerns of their brethren, whether public or personal. He reminds them of the fatal consequences of the unbelief and faint-heartedness of their fathers, when they were, as themselves, just ready to enter Canaan. If men considered as they ought what would be the end of sin, they would be afraid of the beginning of it.
[Num.32.16-Num.32.27]
Verses 16-27
Here is the good effect of plain dealing. Moses, by showing their sin, and the danger of it, brought them to their duty, without murmuring or disputing. All men ought to consider the interests of others as well as their own; the law of love requires us to labour, venture, or suffer for each other as there may be occasion. They propose that their men of war should go ready armed before the children of Israel into the land of Canaan, and that they should not return till the conquest of Canaan was ended. Moses grants their request, but he warns them of the danger of breaking their word. If you fail, you sin against the Lord, and not against your brethren only; God will certainly reckon with you for it. Be sure your sin will find you out. Sin will surely find out the sinner sooner or later. It concerns us now to find our sins out, that we may repent of them, and forsake them, lest they find us out to our ruin.
[Num.32.28-Num.32.42]
Verses 28-42
Concerning the settlement of these tribes, observe, that they built the cities, that is, repaired them. A spirit of selfishness, of seeking our own, not the things of Christ, when each one ought to assist others, is as dangerous as it is common. It is impossible to be sincere in the faith, sensible of the goodness of God, constrained by the love of Christ, sanctified by the power of the Holy Ghost, and yet be indifferent to the progress of religion, and the spiritual success of others, through love of ease, or fear of conflict. Let then your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.

The stages of Israel's journey (verses 1–49)

This chapter looks back over Israel's travels through the wilderness.

It is a history worth remembering.

As the people moved toward Canaan, they were constantly being asked to break camp and move again.

That is also the condition of our lives in this world.

We have no lasting city here.

Most of the changes we make are little more than moving from one part of a desert to another.

Israel sometimes went forward and sometimes seemed to go backward.

Yet all the while, the pillar of cloud and fire directed the journey.

God did not lead them along the shortest route, but he led them along the right one.

The path by which he brings his people to himself is always the best path, though it does not always look the nearest.

Remembering earlier journeys should also remind us of God's care for us, our families and our country.

He has led us, fed us and preserved us throughout our lives.

Very few periods of life can be remembered without recalling both God's goodness and our own ingratitude or disobedience.

His kindness leaves us without excuse for our sins.

We would not want to live through the same years again unless God's grace enabled us to avoid the sins we committed and make better use of the opportunities we missed.

Our wanderings will soon end, and our eternal condition will then be fixed.

How important the present moment is!

Happy are those whom the Lord guides with his counsel now and will finally receive into his glory.

The gospel calls us to that happiness.

Now is the acceptable time. Now is the day of salvation.

Sinners should take hold of the opportunity and flee for refuge to the hope set before them.

Let us use our time to glorify God and serve the people of our generation.

He will lead us safely through the remaining journey into his eternal kingdom.

Israel is warned about the Canaanites (verses 50–56)

As Israel prepared to cross the Jordan, the people faced a renewed temptation to adopt the idols of Canaan.

God warned that sparing those idols or the idolaters would lead to judgment.

By doing so, they would be raising vipers close to their own hearts.

If they made peace with the Canaanites, even temporarily, those who remained would become like irritants in their eyes and thorns in their sides.

We should expect trouble from every sin we willingly indulge.

Whatever we allow to tempt us will eventually torment us.

The Canaanites were to be driven from the land.

But if the Israelites adopted their wicked practices, the Israelites would also be driven out.

Listen and fear.

If we do not drive out sin, sin will drive us out.

If we do not put our sinful desires to death, those desires will destroy our souls.

Verses 1-49
This is a brief review of the travels of the children of Israel through the wilderness. It is a memorable history. In their travels towards Canaan they were continually on the remove. Such is our state in this world; we have here no continuing city, and all our removes in this world are but from one part a desert to another. They were led to and fro, forward and backward, yet were all the while under the direction of the pillar of cloud and fire. God led them about, yet led them the right way. The way God takes in bringing his people to himself is always the best way, though it does not always seem to us the nearest way. Former events are mentioned. Thus we ought to keep in mind the providences of God concerning us and families, us and our land, and the many instances of that Divine care which has led us, and fed us, and kept us all our days hitherto. Few periods of our lives can be thought upon, without reminding us of the Lord's goodness, and our own ingratitude and disobedience: his kindness leaves us without excuse for our sins. We could not wish to travel over again the stages we have passed, unless we could hope, by the grace of God, to shun the sins we then committed, and to embrace such opportunities of doing good as we have let slip. Soon will our wanderings end, and our eternal state be fixed beyond recall; how important then is the present moment! Happy are those whom the Lord now guides with his counsel, and will at length receive to his glory. To this happiness the gospel calls us. Behold now is the accepted time, now is the day of salvation. Let sinners seize the opportunity, and flee for refuge to the hope set before them. Let us redeem our time, to glorify God and serve our generation; and he will carry us safely through all, to his eternal kingdom.
[Num.33.50-Num.33.56]
Verses 50-56
Now that they were to pass over Jordan, they were entering again into temptation to follow idols; and they are threatened that, if they spared either the idols or the idolaters, their sin would certainly be their punishment. They would foster vipers in their own bosoms. The remnant of the Canaanites, if they made any peace with them, though but for a time, would be pricks in their eyes, and thorns in their sides. We must expect trouble and affliction from whatever sin we indulge; that which we are willing should tempt us, will vex us. It was intended that the Canaanites should be put out of the land; but if the Israelites learned their wicked ways, they also would be put out. Let us hear this and fear. If we do not drive out sin, sin will drive us out. If we are not the death of our lusts, our lusts will be the death of our souls.

The boundaries of Canaan (verses 1–15)

Canaan was a relatively small country.

Henry reckons it at about 160 miles long and 50 miles wide within the boundaries described here.

Yet this was the land promised to Abraham, the father of the faithful, and to Israel's descendants.

For many centuries, this small region was the place where God alone was truly known.

It was the Lord's vineyard, a garden enclosed.

Just as small gardens and vineyards can be extraordinarily productive, Canaan's limited area was compensated for by the fruitfulness of its soil.

The whole earth belongs to the Lord, with everything in it.

Still, relatively few people know him and serve him.

Those few are blessed, because they bear fruit for God.

Notice how little of the world he gives even to his chosen people.

People who have their inheritance in heaven have good reason to be content with a small share of this earth.

The little that a righteous person possesses, received with God's love and blessing, is better and brings more comfort than the riches of many wicked people.

The people appointed to divide the land (verses 16–29)

God named the men who would distribute the inheritance among the tribes.

The certainty of Israel's coming victory was so great, since God would fight for the people, that he identified in advance the very men who would be entrusted with dividing the conquered land.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe cities of the Levites.1–8The cities of refuge, The laws about murder.9–34
Cities for the Levites (verses 1–8)

The cities assigned to the priests and Levites served two purposes.

They gave them places to live, and they placed teachers of God's law throughout Israel.

The ceremonial sacrifices of the tabernacle and later the temple were offered in one place.

But teaching God's word, praying and praising him were not confined to one location.

Each tribe gave cities from its own inheritance.

In doing so, each expressed gratitude toward God.

Every tribe also benefited from having Levites nearby, ready to teach the knowledge of the Lord.

No part of the country needed to remain in spiritual darkness.

Under the gospel, those who receive instruction from God's word should share their material blessings with those who teach them (Galatians 6:6).

Congregations should free ministers from distractions that prevent them from attending to the responsibilities of their calling.

Then ministers can give themselves fully to their work.

They should also use opportunities to show kindness, win people's trust and encourage them to listen to God's truth.

The cities of refuge and the law concerning killing (verses 9–34)

The law expressed God's strong hatred of murder and provided a way for murderers to be punished.

In the society described here, a close relative of someone killed could act as the avenger of blood, pursuing a known murderer.

But the law made a crucial distinction.

It did not distinguish a killing committed in sudden rage from one carefully planned in advance: both could be murder.

The distinction was between deliberately striking someone with an instrument likely to kill and causing death without intending it.

Only in the second case did the city of refuge offer protection.

Murder, whatever disguise it wears, defiles a country.

Henry condemns killings that were tolerated or left unpunished under names such as dueling and prizefighting.

There were six cities of refuge.

From any part of Israel, a person could reach one of them in less than a day's journey, Henry says.

A person who caused an accidental death could flee there and remain safe until a fair trial.

If cleared of murder, that person was protected from the avenger of blood.

Yet the person still had to remain inside the city's boundaries until the death of the high priest.

That restriction points us to Christ.

Only the death of the great High Priest brings forgiveness of sins and the sinner's complete freedom.

Henry understands the cities of refuge as clear pictures of the salvation Christ provides.

The Old and New Testaments allude to this provision (Zechariah 9:12; Hebrews 6:18).

He identifies six ways the cities point to the gospel.

First, their high towers offered protection. Christ has been lifted up on the cross and exalted to the Father's right hand as Prince and Savior, bringing repentance and forgiveness.

Second, their roads were made smooth and clear. The path to the Redeemer is open; its true obstacle is the unbelief of the sinful heart.

Third, signs pointed travelers toward the city. Ministers of the gospel are appointed to direct sinners toward Christ.

Fourth, their gates stood open day and night. Christ promises never to turn away anyone who comes to him.

Fifth, each city sustained those who entered it. Believers can live by faith on Christ, whose flesh is true food and whose blood is true drink.

Sixth, the cities offered refuge to everyone who qualified to flee there. The gospel likewise shows no partiality.

No person can claim to be so righteous that God's anger is undeserved.

Nor is any soul excluded from hoping for eternal life through simple faith in God's Son.

The riches of Christ's salvation demand our earnest attention and grateful response.

Chapter Outline
The cities of the Levites. | (1-8) |

Verses 1-8
The cities of the priests and Levites were not only to accommodate them, but to place them, as religious teachers, in several parts of the land. For though the typical service of the tabernacle or temple was only in one place, the preaching of the word of God, and prayer and praise, were not thus confined. These cities were to be given out of each tribe. Each thus made a grateful acknowledgement to God. Each tribe had the benefit of the Levites dwelling amongst them, to teach them the knowledge of the Lord; thus no parts of the country were left to sit in darkness. The gospel provides that he who is taught in the word, should communicate to him that teaches, in all good things, [Gal.6.6] Ga 6:6. We are to free God's ministers from distracting cares, and to leave them at leisure for the duties of their station; so that they may be wholly employed therein, and avail themselves of every opportunity, by acts of kindness, to gain the good-will of the people, and to draw their attention.
[Num.35.9-Num.35.34]
Verses 9-34
To show plainly the abhorrence of murder, and to provide the more effectually for the punishment of the murderer, the nearest relation of the deceased, under the title of avenger of blood, (or the redeemer of blood,) in notorious cases, might pursue, and execute vengeance. A distinction is made, not between sudden anger and malice aforethought, both which are the crime of murder; but between intentionally striking a man with any weapon likely to cause death, and an unintentional blow. In the latter case alone, the city of refuge afforded protection. Murder in all its forms, and under all disguises, pollutes a land. Alas! that so many murders, under the name of duels, prize-fights, &c. should pass unpunished. There were six cities of refuge; one or other might be reached in less than a day's journey from any part of the land. To these, man-slayers might flee for refuge, and be safe, till they had a fair trial. If acquitted from the charge, they were protected from the avenger of blood; yet they must continue within the bounds of the city till the death of the high priest. Thus we are reminded that the death of the great High Priest is the only means whereby sins are pardoned, and sinners set at liberty. These cities are plainly alluded to, both in the Old and New Testament, we cannot doubt the typical character of their appointment. Turn ye to the strong hold, ye prisoners of hope, saith the voice of mercy, [Zech.9.12] Zec 9:12, alluding to the city of refuge. St. Paul describes the strong consolation of fleeing for refuge to the hope set before us, in a passage always applied to the gracious appointment of the cities of refuge, [Heb.6.18] He 6:18. The rich mercies of salvation, through Christ, prefigured by these cities, demand our regard. 1. Did the ancient city rear its towers of safety on high? See Christ raised up on the cross; and is he not exalted at the right hand of his Father, to be a Prince and a Saviour, to give repentance and remission of sins? 2. Does not the highway of salvation, resemble the smooth and plain path to the city of refuge? Survey the path that leads to the Redeemer. Is there any stumbling-block to be found therein, except that which an evil heart of unbelief supplies for its own fall? 3. Waymarks were set up pointing to the city. And is it not the office of the ministers of the gospel to direct sinners to Him? 4. The gate of the city stood open night and day. Has not Christ declared, Him that cometh unto me I will in nowise cast out? 5. The city of refuge afforded support to every one who entered its walls. Those who have reached the refuge, may live by faith on Him whose flesh is meat indeed, and whose blood is drink indeed. 6. The city was a refuge for all. In the gospel there is no respect of persons. That soul lives not which deserves not Divine wrath; that soul lives not which may not in simple faith hope for salvation and life eternal, through the Son of God.

The inheritance of Zelophehad's daughters (verses 1–4)

The leaders of Manasseh pointed out a difficulty.

If Zelophehad's daughters married into another tribe, the land granted to them might eventually leave their ancestral tribe.

The leaders wanted to preserve God's arrangement for the inheritances and prevent future disagreements and disputes.

People who possess property should take similar care.

They ought to settle their affairs and arrange their inheritances so as to prevent quarrels among those who come after them.

Marriage within the tribe (verses 5–12)

God answered their concern.

Those who consult his word because they want to secure their heavenly inheritance will receive not only guidance about what to do, but also his gracious acceptance of their honest search.

God would not allow one tribe to become richer at another's expense.

Each tribe was to keep its own inheritance.

Zelophehad's daughters submitted to that command.

How could they fail to marry well when God himself was directing them?

Henry draws a Christian application.

Those who belong to God's people should be especially careful about the people with whom they enter life's closest and most lasting relationships.

A true believer in Jesus ought to marry someone who also belongs to the Lord.

Our intentions and affections should submit to God's revealed will, particularly in marriage.

God's word allows genuine affection and personal preference.

But it does not approve of uncontrolled passion or an idolatrous attachment that refuses to consider the future.

A person who defies proper authority simply to satisfy desire acts against wisdom, the good of society, happiness in marriage and—most seriously—the religion of Christ.

The closing words of Numbers (verse 13)

[Num.36.1-Num.36.4]
Chapter 36
Chapter Outline
The inheritance of the daughters of Zelophehad. | (1-4) |
The daughters of Zelophehad are to marry in their own tribe. | (5-12) |
Conclusion. | (13) |
Verses 1-4
The heads of the tribe of Manasseh represent the evil which might follow, if the daughters of Zelophehad should marry into any other tribes. They sought to preserve the Divine appointment of inheritances, and that contests and quarrels should not rise among those who should come afterwards. It is the wisdom and duty of those who have estates in the world, to settle them, and to dispose of them, so that no strife and contention may arise. ( [Num.36.5-Num.36.12] Nu 36:5-12)
[Num.36.5-Num.36.12]
Verses 5-12
Those who consult the oracles of God, concerning the making of their heavenly inheritance sure, shall not only be directed what to do, but their inquiries shall be graciously accepted. God would not have one tribe enriched at the expense of another. Each tribe was to keep to its own inheritance. The daughters of Zelophehad submitted to this appointment. How could they fail to marry well, when God himself directed them? Let the people of God learn how suitable and proper it is, like the daughters of Israel, to be united only to their own people. Ought not every true believer Israel, to be united only to their own people. Ought not every true believer in Jesus, to be very attentive in the near and tender relations of life, to be united only to such as are united to the Lord? All our intentions and inclinations ought to be subjected to the will of God, when that is made known to us, and especially in contracting marriage. Although the word of God allows affection and preference in this important relation, it does not sanction that foolish, ungovernable, and idolatrous passion, which cares not what may be the end; but in defiance of authority, determines upon self-gratification. All such conduct, however disguised, is against common sense, the interests of society, the happiness of the marriage relation, and, what is still more evil, against the religion of Christ.
[Num.36.13]
Verse 13
These are the judgments the Lord commanded in the plains of Moab. Most of them related to the settlement in Canaan, into which the Israelites were now entering. Whatever new condition God, by his providence, brings us into, we must beg him to teach us the duties of it, and to enable us to do them, that we may do the work of the day in its day, the duty of a place in its place.
